source_evidence.finding: IAU defines constellations as boundary-defined sky areas, distinguishes formal areas from drawn figures, and lists Lacerta with abbreviation Lac.

NASA describes BL Lacertae as a blazar with a central supermassive black hole, bright disk, and Earth-oriented jet; IXPE and ground telescopes measured polarization and support Compton scattering by electrons as the X-ray mechanism.

articles.factual_and_pedagogical_assessment: The final edit identifies BL Lac as a blazar and active galactic nucleus with a supermassive black hole, disk, and Earth-directed jet, so it no longer equates the whole source with the black hole. The opened NASA source supports the observation and X-ray mechanism claims.

source_evidence.finding: IAU lists Delphinus with abbreviation Del and defines a modern constellation as a bounded area of sky.

NASA identifies Caldwell 42/NGC 7006 as a globular cluster in Delphinus; it says globular clusters contain hundreds of thousands of mutually gravity-bound stars, and that tiny background galaxies look fuzzier and more extended than cluster stars. Intervening dust dims visible light while infrared passes through better.

articles.factual_and_pedagogical_assessment: The final image-reading sentence is now confined to the source-supported distinction between cluster stars and distant background galaxies. The area-versus-cluster and infrared claims remain supported.

source_evidence.finding: IAU lists Triangulum with abbreviation Tri and defines constellation membership through official bounded sky areas.

NASA identifies M33 as a spiral galaxy in Triangulum about 3 million light-years away. Its Hubble page supports the mosaic's stars, clusters, nebulae, blue rapid-star-birth regions, NGC 604 in a spiral arm, and variable-star evidence that M33 is a separate galaxy.

articles.factual_and_pedagogical_assessment: The final text uses neutral «Один из объектов в этой области» and retains source-supported claims about M33, its distance, its separate-galaxy evidence, and the Hubble image.

source_evidence.finding: IAU lists Vulpecula with abbreviation Vul and explains that its official boundaries define a sky area, separate from conventional line figures.

NASA identifies M27 as a planetary nebula in Vulpecula more than 1,200 light-years away; its name comes from a planet-like telescopic appearance, it came from an aging star's shed outer layers, and the displayed Hubble colors map blue to oxygen, green to hydrogen, and red to sulfur and nitrogen.

articles.factual_and_pedagogical_assessment: The article accurately separates the Vulpecula sky area from M27, explains the historical misnomer without calling it a planet, attaches the distance to the nebula, and frames the color mapping as data visualization.
